newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE-Greenspan may spark more flattening.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE-Greenspan may spark more flattening.

text.p: While the weather on Wall Street has been true to form in entering March like a lion, the U.S. Treasury yield curve has acted more like a lamb.

The coupon part of the curve flattened a bit after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned of a pre-emptive strike on inflation during last week's initial leg of his Humphrey Hawkins testimony. But in the week since, the curve has barely moved despite Treasury prices falling for a week.

But should Greenspan maintain his hawkish stance during Wednesday's testimony before the House banking committee, the curve should flatten as it normally does when the market senses increased odds of a rate hike.
"The curve is very steep," noted Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "That makes me believe people are not thinking about a tighthening in March."
Late Tuesday, the two-year note was yielding 6.13 percent while the 30-year bond was at 6.88. The a spread of 75 basis points was the widest it has been since before Greenspan spoke last week.
At the same time, yields across every sector have risen more than 10 basis points each, to levels not seen since late January.
"This is unusual for the market to go down as it has been (in recent days) and to remain as steep as it has been," DeSarno said.
Players, though, said they expect the curve to flatten by about five basis points -- as it did last week -- should the Fed chief reiterate his warning of a "pre-emptive" strike on future inflation.

"Given the (slight) steepening we saw the last couple days, there is potential to get back to where we were last Wednesday after Greenspan" testified before the Senate Banking Committee, said Mary Dennis, senior market economist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. The two-year to 30-year spread had narrowed to 73 basis points, from 76 the day earlier (based on the when-issued bond).

Dennis said she did not expect Greenspan to back off from his tough talk last week, especially in the wake of a strong housing report and upward pressure in the National Association of Purchasing Management's price indexes.

Some traders argued the curve would be much flatter if not for the recent deluge of corporate supply, mostly in 10-year notes and up. Traders reported widespread hedging of Treasuries in longer-dated paper against the more than $3 billion in corporate suppy issued this week so far.

"The market is starting to believe him," said Brett Benza, senior trader at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, referring to Greenspan's tightening suggestions. He noted that prices fell on Tuesday despite such market positives as a coupon pass and friendly remarks from Fed vice chair Alice Rivlin.
"Unless (Greenspan) retracts what he said then the market has turned to a down phase," Benza said, adding that the Fed chair is not likely to change his tune.
DeSarno added that the market is also fearful of a strong February employment report on Friday. So, "the Street is unwilling to take on new positions," he said.

He said that the market will eventually fully price in a tightening. "The last time Greenspan used the word 'pre-emptive' was in January 1994," DeSarno said. "And you know what happened in February (1994)."
